source.title: Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics

confidence_rationale: A causally-manipulated (targeted memory reactivation, TMR) human sleep study directly tests whether cueing difficulty-adjusted, individually-tailored reactivation during sleep improves consolidation for the hardest-to-retain memories, and finds EEG-measurable slow-wave/spindle synchronization tracking behavioral improvement specifically for challenging items. This is direct evidence for MECH-122's packaging-during-slow-wave-sleep framing (spindles as a packaging/consolidation-selection signal) and offers a priority-weighted analogue to MECH-285's staleness/priority mechanism: reactivation frequency adaptively allocated by retrieval difficulty is close to a priority-weighted replay policy operating during the offline phase.
failure_signatures: The 'personalization' here is adaptive STIMULATION FREQUENCY based on behavioral retrieval performance and task difficulty during a word-pair task -- a much narrower, more externally-cued form of priority allocation than MECH-285's staleness-driven internal replay-priority mechanism, which operates without external cueing at all. Treat this as an analogy for the FUNCTION (priority-weighted consolidation), not a mechanistic test of MECH-285's specific staleness signal.

This is a declarative word-pair memory task in healthy young adults with explicit external audio cueing during sleep -- a substantially more externally-scaffolded paradigm than REE's autonomous internal replay architecture; the causal lever here (cue presentation) has no direct REE analogue.

mapping.source_claim_statement: A personalized targeted-memory-reactivation (TMR) protocol that adjusts cueing frequency during sleep based on an individual's retrieval performance and task difficulty significantly reduces memory decay and improves error correction for challenging-to-recall word-pair associations, relative to standard TMR and no-TMR controls; EEG shows enhanced slow-wave/spindle synchronization specifically correlated with behavioral improvement on the challenging items.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-122 frames sleep spindles as a packaging signal for offline consolidation; MECH-285 is REE's staleness/priority mechanism for replay scheduling. Shin et al. supply behavioral and EEG evidence that (a) slow-wave/spindle dynamics causally track successful offline consolidation, supporting MECH-122's packaging framing, and (b) allocating more reactivation resource to harder-to-retain items produces better consolidation than uniform reactivation, which is a human behavioral analogue to a priority-weighted replay policy (MECH-285's functional role), even though the specific priority signal here is external difficulty-cueing rather than REE's internal staleness metric.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The priority signal in this study is EXTERNALLY imposed (experimenter-adjusted cue frequency based on measured retrieval difficulty), not an internally-computed staleness or error signal the way MECH-285 specifies -- this is evidence for the general VALUE of priority-weighted offline consolidation over uniform consolidation, not a direct test of MECH-285's specific staleness-driven mechanism. Similarly, MECH-122's packaging framing is supported at the level of 'spindle dynamics correlate with successful consolidation,' not at the level of a specific packaging algorithm.
mapping.source_context: Human EEG study; healthy young adults; word-pair declarative memory task with audio-cued targeted memory reactivation during a nap, difficulty-adaptive cueing frequency as the experimental manipulation.

confidence_components.notes: Solid peer-reviewed human EEG/behavioral study with a clean causal manipulation (TMR) and a dose/difficulty-adaptive design. Mapping fidelity moderate: supports the general packaging/priority FUNCTIONS MECH-122/MECH-285 propose, but the specific mechanisms (externally-cued difficulty-adaptive reactivation) differ substantially from REE's internally-computed staleness-driven replay scheduling.
